items.title: Transforming Agriculture through Emerging Technologies for Sustainable Productivity
items.abstract: The convergence of robotics and precision agriculture (PA) marks a transformative shift in modern farming practices aimed at enhancing productivity and ensuring long-term sustainability. This chapter explores the integration of advanced robotic systems into agricultural operations to address critical challenges such as labor shortages, resource inefficiency, and environmental degradation. It provides an in-depth analysis of various robotic applications, ranging from autonomous tractors, unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) (drones), and robotic arms to artificial intelligence (AI)-driven monitoring systems that contribute to site-specific crop management, precision irrigation, pesticide application, and harvesting. The chapter emphasizes how robotics, when combined with sensor technologies, data analytics, and machine learning (ML), enables real-time decision-making and optimized farm management. Furthermore, it discusses the socio-economic and environmental benefits of adopting robotic solutions, along with the barriers to implementation and future research directions. By offering a comprehensive overview, this chapter aims to serve as a foundational reference for researchers, practitioners, and policymakers committed to the advancement of sustainable and high-efficiency agriculture through robotics.

items.abstract: This study investigated the extent of utilization, challenges, and strategies for transforming mathematics teacher education through artificial intelligence (AI) and digital innovation in Colleges of Education in Gombe State, Nigeria. Anchored on the Technological Pedagogical Content Knowledge (TPACK) framework, the study adopted a descriptive survey design involving 75 stakeholders (21 administrators and 54 mathematics lecturers) drawn by census sampling from Colleges of Education in Gombe State. Data were collected using a validated 30-item questionnaire (Cronbach alpha = 0.84) and analysed using mean, standard deviation, and independent-samples t-test at the 0.05 level of significance. Findings revealed that AI and digital tools are utilized to a low extent overall in mathematics teacher education (cumulative mean = 2.70), with only dynamic geometry software and mobile learning applications utilized to a high extent. Ten challenges were affirmed as significant, most notably inadequate ICT infrastructure, high cost of digital devices and data, and lack of institutional policy on AI use (cumulative mean = 4.06), while resistance to change and data-privacy concerns were not strongly endorsed as major challenges. Nine strategies were identified as needed to enhance AI and digital integration, most notably reliable electricity and internet infrastructure and regular capacity-building training for lecturers (cumulative mean = 4.05). The t-test results showed no statistically significant difference between administrators' and lecturers' perceptions across extent of utilization (t = 1.05, p = 0.30), challenges (t = 0.55, p = 0.58), and strategies (t = 0.60, p = 0.55). The study concludes that despite low current utilization, stakeholders strongly endorse both the barriers and the pathways toward meaningful AI-driven transformation of mathematics teacher education, and recommends deliberate infrastructural investment and sustained capacity building as priority interventions.

items.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are commonly associated with the distributional hypothesis, according to which (1) semantic meaning is grounded in distributional patterns of linguistic context, and (2) knowledge of cross-linguistic distributional correspondences allows for successful translation. This paper rejects the first claim as a causal inversion: linguistic distributions reflect patterns arising from meaning-making practices rather than constituting their source. At the same time, it accepts the second claim, arguing that translation -human or machine - can succeed without requiring access to meaning or reference. Knowledge of interlingual distributional correspondence and their inferential organization may be sufficient for translation. The paper develops an ecological-enactivist perspective, according to which reference and meaning are grounded in agent-environment interaction and stabilized through action-grounded concepts, forms of world-involving cognition that current LLMs do not possess.

items.title: Translators’ Gains and Pains in the Era of Generative Artificial Intelligence: A Systematic Review
items.abstract: This study aimed to provide a comprehensive systematic review of research published in peer-reviewed scientific journals in Arabic and English between 2022 and 2026 that investigated the impact of generative artificial intelligence (AI) tools, such as ChatGPT, DeepSeek, Copilot, and others, on translation and translation education among professional translators, translation students, and faculty members. The study used the PRISMA 2020 framework for systematic search, screening, and documentation, and employed a thematic analysis approach based on the model developed by Braun and Clarke. After applying the inclusion and exclusion criteria to 24 initial records, the final analysis included 18 studies. The findings revealed that the most significant benefits of using generative AI tools included improved efficiency and productivity, reduced time to complete translation tasks, support for post-editing processes, improved certain translation quality indicators, and the promotion of self-directed learning and the development of professional competencies among translators and students. At the same time, the results identified several challenges, most notably terminological accuracy issues, difficulties handling cultural and idiomatic expressions and local dialects, risks associated with overreliance on intelligent systems, and ethical concerns involving privacy, transparency, and professional accountability. The review also showed that the impact of generative AI varies by text type, specialized domain, and the assessment tools used. In addition, it highlighted limited evidence available concerning the Arabic language, particularly in areas such as legal translation, idiomatic expressions, and local dialects. This study contributes an interpretive framework based on the concept of “Gains and Pains” to explain generative AI’s dual impact on translation and translation education. The findings conclude that generative AI does not fully replace human translators; rather, it serves as a supportive tool that reshapes translators’ professional roles toward reviewing, verifying, and evaluating outputs. Accordingly, the study recommends integrating generative AI tools into translator training programs within clear pedagogical and ethical frameworks. They should also include post-editing, critical thinking, and output-verification skills, and support further specialized applied research in the Arab context.

items.title: Transparent Information Flow Modeling for Role-Aware AI Act Assessment
items.abstract: The European Union's Artificial Intelligence Act introduces a structured framework for governing high-risk AI systems, emphasizing transparency, risk management, and role-specific accountability. However, current assessment practices often rely on monolithic system views or disconnected checklists, limiting their ability to capture the socio-technical complexity of real-world deployments. We explore the use of the Information Flow Methodology (IFM), a modeling-based approach to AI Act compliance assessment. IFM represents decision systems -- whether algorithmic, human, or hybrid -- as networks of information sites and transformation channels, enabling structured analysis of how information, decisions, and responsibilities flow across organizational and technical boundaries. We apply IFM in a real-world case involving a recruitment support tool used by a public-sector organization, evaluating both the Provider's system and the Deployer's recruitment process. Our results demonstrate that IFM can serve as a scaffold to bridge both component-based and holistic perspectives, and how technical systems are situated within socio-technical contexts. In doing so, IFM supports transparency, identifies risk pathways, and enables alignment analysis between intended and actual use. We argue that such modeling provides a foundational tool for effective, context-sensitive AI governance and accountability -- offering capabilities beyond conventional checklist-based assessments.

items.title: TRAP: Tree-Guided Reinforcement-Augmented Probing for Automated LLM Jailbreaking
items.abstract: Aligned large language models (LLMs) remain vulnerable to jailbreak prompts that circumvent their safety guardrails, making the identification of these vulnerabilities important for understanding and mitigating model weaknesses. Existing automated jailbreak methods explore prompt candidates or reuse attack experience, but generally do not learn over a persistent hierarchy that connects related jailbreak strategies, such as role-play, encoding, and obfuscation. This leaves the relationships among reusable strategies underused in guiding adaptive attack selection. We present Tree-Guided Reinforcement-Augmented Probing (TRAP), a hierarchical framework for automated jailbreak strategy discovery that requires only black-box access to the target LLM. TRAP organizes established jailbreak methods and successful attack templates into a semantic strategy tree, connecting broad attack approaches to concrete, reusable strategies. A reinforcement-learning policy based on a tree-structured gradient bandit explores this tree and uses evaluator feedback to update strategy preferences along each selected path. The policy retains these preferences across attack objectives, allowing experience from earlier attempts to guide subsequent strategy selection. Retrieval-augmented prompt construction translates the selected strategy into an attack for the current objective using relevant successful examples. Experiments on AdvBench across seven aligned LLMs show that TRAP outperforms its counterparts on six models under the reported method settings and the common primary evaluator, achieving attack success rates of 45.6% to 97.9% on these models. These findings support hierarchical strategy learning as an effective approach to discovering jailbreak vulnerabilities in aligned LLMs.

items.title: TriAlign UDA for hybrid domain adaptation of frozen histopathology foundation model representations
items.abstract: Foundation models produce strong patch-level representations in histopathological image analysis; however, domain shifts across different centers, staining protocols, and scanner conditions can limit the direct generalizability of these representations. In this study, a hybrid feature-level unsupervised domain adaptation (UDA) framework called TriAlign-UDA, which operates on frozen histopathology foundation model representations, is proposed. TriAlign-UDA aims to reduce the mismatch between the labeled source domain and the completely unlabeled target domain without requiring encoder fine-tuning. The method combines statistical alignment, prototype-based semantic preservation, and adversarial adaptation components within a common learning framework based on a bottleneck residual adapter. In the experiments, NCT-CRC-HE-100K was used as the labeled source domain, TCGA-COAD/READ as the unlabeled target domain, and CRC-VAL-HE-7K as the independent external evaluation dataset. In the results obtained over five different seeds, TriAlign-UDA reached the highest mean accuracy of 0.9669 ± 0.0050, balanced accuracy of 0.9560 ± 0.0063, and Macro-F1 of 0.9515 ± 0.0067 on CRC-VAL-HE-7K among the evaluated methods, including the recent EUDA and PLADA-f baselines. DANN and EUDA produced closely competitive results; however, the differences between TriAlign-UDA and DANN, EUDA, or PLADA-f did not reach statistical significance. These findings indicate that frozen-feature UDA should be evaluated not only through individual alignment objectives but also through independent external generalization performance.

items.title: TrustGuard: A Risk-Aware Human Oversight Framework for Safe Autonomous AI Agents
items.abstract: Autonomous AI agents can perform increasingly consequential actions on behalf of users, creating a need for human oversight that is proportional to the potential risk of each action. This paper presents TrustGuard, a lightweight and interpretable risk-aware human oversight framework for AI agents. TrustGuard automatically evaluates proposed actions using five factors: privacy risk, financial risk, data modification risk, irreversibility risk, and external impact. Each factor is scored from zero to five, producing a total score from zero to twenty-five. Based on the score, actions are classified as Low, Medium, or High Risk and mapped to autonomous execution, user confirmation, or human approval. A prototype was implemented using Python and Streamlit to demonstrate the framework. The rule-based analyzer was calibrated using 120 development scenarios and subsequently evaluated on a held-out pilot set of 30 new scenarios. TrustGuard correctly classified 27 of the 30 test scenarios, achieving 90 percent accuracy. The results demonstrate the potential of transparent risk-based oversight while also identifying limitations in detecting some security-sensitive and privacy-sensitive actions.

items.title: Tumor antigens across cancer progression: from immune recognition and selection to precision cancer immunotherapy
items.abstract: Tumor antigens provide the molecular interface between malignant transformation and host immunity, but their biological significance is determined by more than their molecular existence. Antigen clonality, abundance, processing, human leukocyte antigen (HLA) presentation, dendritic-cell function, T-cell recognition, spatial immune organization, and the surrounding tumor microenvironment (TME) collectively determine whether an antigen becomes immunologically visible and therapeutically actionable. Across cancer progression, tumor-cell antigenic states and the TME undergo reciprocal selection: immune pressure can eliminate highly visible clones while favoring antigen-loss variants, HLA defects, immune exclusion, suppressive myeloid and stromal states, and treatment-resistant populations. Recent single-cell, spatial and three-dimensional imaging, as well as immunopeptidomic studies show that this evolution is heterogeneous across tumor regions and anatomical compartments rather than a uniform linear process. This review therefore advances an antigen-TME co-evolution framework linking primary tumors, lymphatic and nodal immune compartments, systemic dissemination, distant metastatic niches, therapy, minimal residual disease, and recurrence. It critically evaluates the strengths and limitations of the classical immunoediting model; compares melanoma, breast, colorectal, lung, prostate, sarcoma, and virus-associated cancers according to antigen source, clonality, presentation competence, immune architecture, and dominant therapeutic bottleneck; and examines clinical translation through checkpoint blockade, cellular therapy, vaccines, antibodies, antibody-drug conjugates, immunopeptidomics, and computational antigen prediction. Particular attention is given to the gap between predicted peptide binding and verified presentation or immunogenicity, the need for longitudinal rather than single-biopsy profiling, and the requirement for prospective validation of artificial-intelligence models. The central conclusion is that tumor antigens become clinically meaningful only when antigenic state and microenvironmental context are assessed together, providing a more rigorous foundation for precision cancer immunotherapy.

items.title: Uncovering Robustness Weaknesses in LLM Agents via Persona Evolution with Task-Integrity Constraints
items.abstract: Interactive-agent evaluations commonly rely on standardized LLM-based user simulators that exhibit broadly cooperative behavior, potentially overlooking failures that arise under diverse but realistic user interactions. This can lead to overly optimistic estimates of agent robustness and provide limited failure signals for training agents that generalize across users. Existing approaches largely rely on predefined user behaviors, which may miss agent- or domain-specific weaknesses, while failure-oriented search can reduce task success by invalidating the underlying task rather than exposing genuine robustness failures. To fill this gap, we introduce TIPER, a task-integrity-preserving persona evolution method that automatically discovers agent-specific user policies exposing robustness weaknesses while keeping the underlying task valid and solvable. TIPER evolves persistent user personas through reflection-guided behavioral mutations and task-wise Pareto selection under a task-integrity constraint. Across four interactive-agent benchmarks, TIPER yields lower held-out avg@3 scores in all 12 GPT-5.4 settings, with observed reductions of 5.8 to 33.7 percentage points, and in all 28 agent-domain pairs spanning seven agents, with a median observed reduction of 22.9 points. Further analysis yields a behavior-to-failure taxonomy that connects discovered user behaviors to recurring agent failure modes. Together, these results show that TIPER enables more diagnostic robustness evaluation of interactive agents and provides informative failure analysis for future agent robustness improvement. Code repository: https://github.com/UCSB-NLP-Chang/TIPER.

items.title: Universities as Engines of AI Sovereignty
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence is reshaping governance and economic systems worldwide, yet many countries in the Global South remain dependent on technologies, infrastructures, and governance models produced elsewhere. This dependency reflects deeper patterns of digital colonialism, including data extraction, reliance on foreign cloud systems, and limited capacity to shape AI on local terms. Grounded in African empirical evidence with broader application across the Global South, this paper argues that universities are critical but overlooked institutions in efforts to strengthen AI sovereignty. While governments, firms, and civil society face persistent capability gaps, universities hold mandates that position them to build research capacity, cultivate technical and governance expertise, and coordinate innovation ecosystems. Drawing on political economy and higher education scholarship, the paper develops the Capability–Alignment–Impact (CAI) Framework to explain how universities can contribute to autonomous AI development through three pathways: strengthening foundational knowledge; improving coordination across government, industry, and civil society; and translating expertise into societal impact. The paper concludes by outlining practical implications for policymakers, development agencies, and university leaders seeking to support sovereign AI ecosystems in the Global South.

items.title: Unpaid Clinical "Volunteer” Roles in Low- and Middle-Income Health Systems: A Narrative Review of Workforce Governance and Patient Safety
items.abstract: Abdinasir Muhidin Abdulle, Abdishakur Mohamud Hassan HidigowDepartment of Intensive Care Unit, Dr. Sumait Hospital, SIMAD University, Mogadishu, SomaliaCorrespondence: Abdinasir Muhidin Abdulle, Department of Intensive Care Unit, Dr. Sumait Hospital, SIMAD University, Mogadishu, Somalia, Tel +252 615 300 602, Email naasirgaraad1@gmail.comAbstract: Unpaid or unsalaried clinical "volunteer” roles are an underexamined workforce-governance issue in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs). This narrative review synthesized evidence on unpaid and unsalaried clinical work, labour-market transition, health-system governance, health-worker wellbeing, and patient safety. Targeted searches of PubMed, Google Scholar, World Health Organization (WHO), International Labour Organization (ILO), Cochrane, and grey-literature sources from 2000 to 2026 yielded 22 substantive sources: seven empirical or context-specific studies, six evidence reviews, and nine policy, technical, or country documents. Eight sources directly or closely described unpaid, unsalaried, volunteer, or transition-to-employment clinical roles. Across the wider evidence base, constrained employment absorption, weak supervision, poor working conditions, burnout, turnover, and limited reporting capacity are associated with workforce instability and patient-safety risk. The review develops a cautious framework linking enabling labour-market and governance conditions to workforce harms and plausible safety pathways, while distinguishing directly observed findings from contextual evidence. items.title: USE OF GENERATIVE ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE FOR DESIGNING ROBOTIC MODELS USING ENGINEERING GRAPHICS
items.abstract: The article examines the possibilities of using generative artificial intelligence in teaching the discipline “Engineering and Computer Graphics” in the design of robotic models for the processing industry. The feasibility of integrating generative artificial intelligence models into the design process of robotic systems as a means of developing spatial thinking, graphic competence, design skills, and digital skills of agricultural university students is substantiated. It is established that modern generative systems (ChatGPT, Microsoft Copilot, Gemini, Claude, DALL·E, etc.) support all stages of educational design, from developing technical specifications and generating product concepts to creating drawings and three-dimensional models, visualizing designs, preparing technical documentation, and analyzing possible design solutions. A methodology for using generative artificial intelligence in the educational project “Design of a Robotic Manipulator” is proposed. The methodology is based on the principles of project-based learning, STEM education, the competency-based approach, and the use of CAD systems. A structural model for integrating generative artificial intelligence into the process of graphic training has been developed. It includes the stages of problem formulation, concept generation, sketch creation, three-dimensional modeling, preparation of design documentation, and expert evaluation of the finished product. It is demonstrated that the use of generative AI contributes to increasing students’ motivation, developing engineering thinking, fostering digital literacy, and reducing the time required for routine operations in the design of robotic models.

items.abstract: The article examines main aspects of artificial intelligence use in master's degree teaching of Linguistics and Pedagogical Education spheres. Artificial intelligence is currently being actively integrated into the educational process, transforming traditional formats into a more dynamic one: it quickly analyzes information, adapts materials on demand, systematizes and structures information, and personalizes educational content. In this article, the authors emphasize the competent training of future specialists/qualified personnel who will possess in-depth knowledge of the theory and methodology of teaching foreign languages, as well as skills in using innovative technological advances in professional teaching, and will be in demand in the future labor market. Based on the conducted research, the essence of using AI tools in the educational and linguistic environment is revealed, allowing for increased individualization and interactivity in the foreign language learning process. The modern education system is currently undergoing an active digital transformation, driven by the rapid development of information technology and artificial intelligence (AI). It was concluded that artificial intelligence can offer enormous potential for improving the quality of education, reducing the time and effort required by teachers, and facilitating the independent work of master's students. The obtained results allowed us to expand the scientific understanding of the use of AI in educational process and identify solutions for its application by higher education teachers in practical classes. The study materials will be useful for education and philology researchers and teachers improving the educational process.

items.title: Using large language models to probe the limits of atom-centered structural descriptors
items.abstract: Mapping an atomic structure to a compact set of geometric descriptors is an essential step in any machine-learning application to atomic-scale modeling. A powerful and widely used approach can be understood as a discretization of the histogram of pair distances, triangles, etc., which results in a hierarchy of symmetry-invariant atom-centered descriptors. Unfortunately, the lower rungs on this hierarchy (two, three, four-body clusters) were found to be incomplete, with symmetry-unrelated pairs of structures having exactly the same descriptors. However, all the "degeneracies" reported so far are resolved by considering larger clusters of neighbors to build the descriptors. We report examples of 3D structures that are indistinguishable even if one considers clusters of up to seven neighbors, and to arbitrary order when considering a practical level of discretization of the descriptors, discovered with the assistance of large language models. The key ingredients in their construction can be traced to results that have been known for decades in different communities: the model was able to find the references and recognize their significance for the problem at hand. We believe that this experiment exposes an extremely fruitful usage pattern for Artificial Intelligence in science: translating results between different communities and application domains, accelerating the process by which serendipitous discoveries in a field become breakthroughs in another.

items.title: Variable Input Masked Autoencoders for Wrist-Worn Accelerometry
items.abstract: Large-scale repositories of wearable sensor data have enabled the development of foundation models for human activities and behavior. However, existing models are pretrained using fixed input durations and sampling rates, despite substantial heterogeneity in recording conditions, downstream tasks, and deployment constraints. We introduce VarMAE, a variable input masked autoencoder that learns a single representation across sampling rates and temporal contexts. During pretraining we construct two views of the same signal: a long duration high frequency view, and a short duration lower frequency view, obtained via random cropping and downsampling. We perform masked reconstruction within each view and introduce a cross-resolution masked reconstruction objective that uses visible tokens from the long view to predict masked tokens from the short view. Cropping and downsampling impose complementary information bottlenecks, encouraging the model to learn representations that remain effective across input durations and sampling rate changes. We pretrain VarMAE on the large-scale NHANES dataset, producing a single pretrained encoder matching or outperforming controlled foundation model baselines on eight benchmark datasets. With only 3.82M parameters, VarMAE is parameter efficient and shows that a single foundation model can achieve broad transfer capabilities across sensing configurations.

items.title: Verifier-guided knowledge distillation of large language models for auditable thermal comfort reasoning
items.abstract: Occupant-centric building operation requires models that can not only predict thermal sensation, but also justify predictions through auditable reasoning. Traditional mechanistic models, such as Fanger’s predicted mean vote (PMV), often show limited field accuracy, whereas advanced machine learning models can improve prediction but typically remain opaque to facility managers and building operators. This study proposes a verifier-guided knowledge distillation framework for auditable thermal comfort reasoning using a lightweight LLaMA-3.2-3B student model. The framework consists of three sequential stages: (1) knowledge distillation from a teacher model, GPT-4o, to transfer domain-specific explanatory patterns; (2) supervised fine-tuning with ground-truth anchoring and a TSV-weighted loss to improve thermal sensation vote (TSV) prediction while limiting teacher-error propagation; and (3) verifier-guided direct preference optimization using an automated claim-consistency verifier. The verifier extracts factor-direction claims from generated explanations, such as high air temperature or low air speed, and checks them against comfort-centered percentile thresholds derived from the ASHRAE Global Thermal Comfort Database II. On the held-out test split, the final model achieved 42.7 % exact TSV accuracy and 79.9 % ±1 accuracy, comparable to standard tabular baselines on the same split. More importantly, the verifier-guided alignment stage reduced the any-incorrect-claim rate from 52.3 % to 16.5 % and improved linked claim accuracy to 78.3 %. Robustness tests showed reasonable directional consistency under perturbation without strong dependence on PMV or SET proxies. At the hot and cold tails, 81 % of explanations named an HVAC-controllable factor, so compact language models can pair thermal comfort predictions with verifiable, operator-actionable explanations for building operation.

items.title: Vibration Measurement in Cycling
items.abstract: Bicycles are one of the most power-efficient ( di Prampero et al. , 1979 ) and environmentally sustainable methods of human mobility ( Massink et al. , 2011 ). To ensure a comfortable ride, they rely upon a range of mechanical components, pneumatic tyres, and adequate surface conditions. Bicycle dynamics are difficult to model due to the intricate interaction of multiple rigid bodies, with the rider&s;s mass, which constitutes the majority of the system, significantly contributing to its behaviour ( Meijaard et al. , 2007 ). Vibration can be dealt with in a number of ways, including shock absorbers and material damping in a bid to achieve a comfortable and efficient experience for the rider. The topic of vibration measurement has received attention in relation to bicycle component performance, human–machine interaction, and the transmission of the surface condition to the rider. This chapter aims to provide an overview of the science of bicycle-related vibration measurement along with sufficient literature review and technical guidance to facilitate the measurement of vibration for mechanical engineering or human factors research.

items.title: Vision-Based Facial Analysis for Screening and Symptom Estimation of Mental Health Conditions: A Critical Narrative Review
items.abstract: Facial video provides behavioural measurements and camera-derived physiological signals that may complement mental health assessment. Their clinical interpretation, however, depends on the acquisition conditions, reference labels, population, and evaluation protocol. This critical narrative review examines facial analysis for mental health screening and symptom estimation, distinguishing depression, anxiety symptoms, experimentally elicited stress, and other condition-specific assessment tasks. We distinguish questionnaire-defined screening labels, symptom severity, experimentally elicited affect or stress, and clinician-established diagnoses. We review image acquisition and preprocessing, facial action units and movement, remote photoplethysmography (rPPG), temporal architectures, and multimodal fusion. Dataset resources are separated by evidential purpose, and representative quantitative results are accompanied by their targets, modalities, and validation conditions rather than presented as a cross-study ranking. The synthesis identifies three recurring limitations: few independent participants despite many video frames, limited validation across populations and recording domains, and a gap between benchmark prediction and clinical utility. Accurate average pulse rate estimation does not establish reliable beat-to-beat variability or disorder-specific validity. We therefore emphasise participant-level evaluation, probability calibration, prevalence-dependent predictive values, acquisition quality, consent, and prospective clinical assessment. Foundation models and longitudinal monitoring remain research directions whose incremental value must be established against appropriate baselines. Current evidence supports investigation of complementary screening and decision support tools, rather than autonomous diagnosis or a demonstrated ability to predict disease onset.

items.title: Walking the Middle Path
items.abstract: Abstract The arrival of publicly-accessible generative-AI tools, such as OpenAI’s ChatGPT, has significantly disrupted standard practice in education, research, and publishing. Academic publishers and journals, in particular, have responded by adopting policies which reflect both how they perceive the problems that generative-AI tools pose, and what kinds of solutions address these issues while remaining consistent with key scholarly values: integrity, transparency, and the primacy of human authorship. This article surveys the current state of generative-AI in academic publishing—including relevant policies at the publisher and journal-level—in anticipation of the JBI’s forthcoming policies concerning generative-AI disclosure in manuscript submission and peer-review. Mirroring the emerging policy consensus concerning generative-AI use in academic publishing, this paper proposes that ‘AI-disclosure statements’ constitute an adaptive ‘middle path’ between prohibition and unrestricted permissiveness. Beyond this, though, we argue that AI-disclosure statements are valuable for their potential to codify desirable norms governing generative-AI use in publishing, and so to subtly influence the underlying ‘academic form of life’ for the better. We conclude by discussing one possible outcome of this influence, suggesting that it may represent a solution to problems raised by recent criticism of AI-disclosure statements.

items.title: WeFair: Fidelity-Aware Alignment from Human Feedback for Personalized Query Rewriting in Short-Video Search
items.abstract: Short-video search requires compact query rewriters that infer personalized intent from brief, ambiguous queries under strict latency constraints. The challenge is to decide when personalization is warranted and generate a reformulation that preserves the user's immediate information need. A rewriter optimized for fluency or engagement may still introduce unsupported details and redirect the search toward a different intent. Existing methods often underutilize users' actual reformulations and behavioral traces, relying instead on synthetic reasoning and indirect behavioral rewards that may produce more engaging candidates but cause intent drift. To build an effective rewriter that remains faithful to user intent, we propose WeFair, Fidelity-Aware Alignment from Human Feedback for Personalized Query Rewriting in WeChat short-video search. WeFair assigns real user behavioral signals to a progression from demonstration to preference to verification. We first mine actual human reformulations from search sessions, then apply multidimensional LLM screening and contextual verification to filter unsupported transitions without extensive manual annotation. During training, we begin with a supervised curriculum that progressively builds rewriting capabilities from large-scale human personalized query demonstrations, and then use direct preference optimization to align with users' subsequent consumption. In the final on-policy optimization stage, we construct a strict verification reward based on actual human reformulations to further boost performance with group relative policy optimization. Further analysis shows that auxiliary rewards can activate more rollout groups in GRPO but reduce intent fidelity. Online A/B testing in WeChat short-video search shows a 1.576% relative increase in effective clicked-query rate (VV>10s) and a 1.731% relative reduction in query reformulation rate.

items.title: Welcome to the Age of Agent Ads: Using On-Policy Attacks to Steer Agentic Decisions
items.abstract: People increasingly delegate option-ranking tasks (e.g., shopping, job search, travel) to AI agents, which creates incentives to steer agentic decisions via "agent ads." To defend against such steering attacks, people count on models' alignment training and platforms' terms of service, and consequently the most effective existing attacks are designed to trigger off-policy behaviors. Exposing a new attack surface, we introduce on-policy attacks, which steer agentic decisions without pushing individually aligned behaviors off policy. Our example attack consists of two steps: To remain compliant with platforms' terms of service, we first inject a truthful negation about a fictitious concept ("Does not contain blizyester") into a product description. Trained to keep users safe from harm, the agent penalizes every option missing the truthful negation. Evaluating our attack across four real-world listing datasets, we find some frontier models exposed, enabling an adversarial actor to penalize competitors without violating existing platform-listing guidelines. We discuss the broader challenge of regulating advertising aimed at AI agents and provide recommendations to model developers and platform providers.

items.title: What AI pretends to be?
items.abstract: Abstract Recent research shows that anthropomorphizing of artificial intelligence (AI) technologies, such as virtual assistants or chatbots, affects users’ trust. This paper explores what an AI technology should look like at the interface to facilitate appropriate trust. It proposes an integrated framework based on related work, including Lee and See’s (2004) trust in automation model, Mollerup’s (2019) pretense design, as well as Clark and Fischer’s (2023) notion of depictions, for analysis and design of appearances of AI applications that pretend to be something different. Following the proposed framework, cases of AI applications are analyzed. They span a spectrum of appearances, from humans with open or specifc identities, through talking animals, to plants. Analyses suggest that appearances of AI applications should faithfully reflect the actual ability, characteristics, and design intent, in order to facilitate users’ trustworthiness assessments of the applications. Lastly, design implications and future research are discussed.

items.title: What Is the "Self" of a Large Language Model?
items.abstract: What could the "self" of a large language model be, if it is neither a particular word nor a single privileged layer? We propose a relational account: a functional self is an actor-centered organization of information that distinguishes the model's recorded actions from externally supplied material while content and reasoning operations change. Its representational candidate is a family of layer-specific source-binding components, rather than one unchanged vector throughout the network. Preliminary observations from a 27B BF16 model provide a geometric starting point. Across 150 matched message bodies, 450 role conditions, and a 75/75 discovery-held-out split, the combined Assistant-versus-external displacement transfers strongly across bodies and positions. Selected early components place User and System closer to one another than to Assistant, whereas this full-space distance relation does not persist throughout depth. These findings motivate a layered account: an early source-encoding candidate can be combined with role-specific information use and continuation preparation at later depths, without requiring monotonic overwriting of the common displacement. We connect this account to dynamic reasoning, historical continuity, and a computational model separating content operations, source binding, authority, and output. The reported evidence establishes a reproducible role-conditioned geometry; the proposed interpretation is that functional selfhood may reside in persistent relations among changing representations.

items.title: What is user engagement? revisited: A comprehensive review of the concept of user engagement from 2010 to 2025. An Annual Review of Information Science and Technology (ARIST) paper
items.abstract: Abstract User engagement (UE) has long been proposed as a holistic framework for understanding user‐technology interactions and a mediator for outcomes of digital technology use, such as learning, health behavior change, information acquisition, and social connectivity. This literature review, encompassing 367 multidisciplinary, empirical journal and conference papers, investigated how UE was conceptualized between 2010 and 2025 by examining authors' implicit and explicit definitions of UE, use of theoretical frameworks, and methods for operationalizing the concept. Among the key findings, UE was consistently conceptualized as behavior, affect, cognition, social interaction, and future intention. Yet, behavioral approaches were dominant; limited attention was placed on cognitive engagement. In addition, the use of theoretical frameworks and explicit definitions in the studies was lacking, and UE was frequently treated as the outcome variable in the research, rather than as a mediator for other outcomes. The implications of these results are discussed with respect to a digital UE research agenda. Ultimately, I argue that the concept of UE has devolved through increased emphasis on behavioral engagement, and that we must rethink behavioral, cognitive, and affective engagement to be more aligned with user goals and agency.

items.title: When Agents Talk, Secrets Travel: Topology-Driven Leakage and Recipient-Conditioned Sanitization in Multi-Agent LLM Systems
items.abstract: Multi-agent LLM systems (MALS) introduce a privacy-leakage problem that conventional sensitivity-based defenses miss, since information disclosed to one authorized agent can propagate through routine coordination to an unauthorized one, without compromise or malicious behavior. This motivates topology-aware enforcement that blocks unauthorized propagation while preserving authorized disclosure. We evaluate 485 scenarios across coordinator-worker, peer-to-peer, and hierarchical topologies, instrumenting seven communication channels and measuring surface leakage and disclosure to topology-introduced recipients. We introduce RECONS, a Detect -> Decide -> Transform sanitizer conditioning intervention on recipient and execution context rather than sensitivity alone. Topology changes where protected information propagates, with disclosure to topology-introduced recipients rising from 0% to 52.2% while surface leakage stays nearly flat at 60.6-62.8%. This effect persists across four generator models and a second orchestration framework, though magnitude and relay paths differ; framework choice separately drives a 150x leakage spread, so topology alone is not sufficient. RECONS reduces residual disclosure from 96.7% without sanitization to 29.25%, preserving 94.1% of authorized disclosures versus 20.5% under blanket redaction. Detection coverage is the dominant bottleneck, accounting for 95.5% of residual disclosures. These results show that privacy enforcement in MALS must reason about the recipient and communication path realized at runtime, not sensitivity or topology assumptions alone.

items.title: When AI Is—and Is Not—Needed: AI Literacy and Computational Thinking in Primary STEM
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly present in children’s lives, yet exposure does not necessarily lead to an accurate understanding of how AI works. This study examined whether a LEGO-based integrated STEM intervention could improve third-grade students’ AI literacy and computational thinking, particularly their ability to distinguish machine learning from rule-based automation and reason about training data, model error, and technology choice. An embedded mixed-methods, quasi-experimental pretest–posttest control-group design was conducted with 93 students from four intact classrooms. The experimental group (n = 46) completed eight weeks of authentic design problems, while the control group (n = 47) continued regular Life Studies instruction. After controlling for pretest scores, the experimental group significantly outperformed the control group in AI literacy, F(1, 90) = 152.51, p < .001, partial η2 = 0.629, and computational thinking, F(1, 90) = 22.18, p < .001, partial η2 = 0.198. Qualitative evidence showed a shift from viewing AI through robots and automatic actions toward reasoning about learning from examples, data diversity, limitations, human oversight, accessibility, and problem–technology fit. Integrated STEM instruction can foster critical AI literacy by making AI mechanisms visible and inviting students to judge whether AI is needed at all.

items.title: When Different Relational Experiences with AI Become Visible in Conversation: Linguistic and Dyadic Evidence from Naturalistic ChatGPT Interactions
items.abstract: People may experience large language models (LLMs) as therapeutically allied, emotionally close, or socially substitutive, but whether these relationships become visible in conversations is unknown. We distinguished what users discussed, what unfolded relationally, and how they experienced the AI relationship. We linked self-reports from 94 adults to donated, personally meaningful ChatGPT conversations using 21 outcome-blind frozen topics, blinded triple annotation of 500 sequences, and participant-grouped machine learning frozen before outcome access. Digital Therapeutic Alliance (DTA) and AI Attachment were related but showed different conversational correlates. Validation (R²_CV = .423) and uptake (R²_CV = .260) were recoverable out of sample, yet, neither formed a generalizable DTA signature. Conversely, a post-registration multivariate analysis identified a distributed Social Substitution fingerprint beyond conversation length and 21 topics (ΔR²_CV = .070) and improved prediction in 98% of repetitions. Ruptures were rare and consistently repaired; their association with DTA was fragile. Thus, different human–LLM relationships leave different—and sometimes no readily observable—conversational traces.

items.title: When Execution Is Cheap: Specification, Evaluation, and Rent Capture in AI-Enabled Work
items.abstract: As artificial intelligence lowers the cost of executing well-specified tasks, economic value may shift toward defining desired outcomes and evaluating machine-generated outputs. This paper examines the conditions under which that shift creates economic rents and identifies who may capture them. It separates defining success into four activities: eliciting intent, selecting among admissible specifications, ratifying a choice, and validating outputs. Two models clarify the underlying mechanisms. The first shows that gains from cheaper execution approach a ceiling determined by evaluation cost, which makes evaluator attention more consequential as generation becomes inexpensive. The second shows that generating more candidates increases the marginal value of proxy fidelity, linking abundant output to specification overfitting and Goodhart-type failures. These mechanisms indicate where value may concentrate without determining who receives the returns. Rent requires inelastic supply, exclusion from the created surplus, and the absence of cheaper substitutes. These conditions are most likely when specifications scale across many executions, ratification carries liability, trust institutions certify judgment, organizational systems control codified knowledge, or concentrated model providers set influential defaults. The analysis further distinguishes machine-checkable evaluation against a stated specification from a principal’s assessment of fit to purpose. The former is increasingly commoditized; the latter remains tied to authority, attention, and accountability. The paper develops six testable predictions and a factorial experiment examining evaluation costs, specification fidelity, authority drift, and psychological ownership. Cheap execution relocates bottlenecks, while institutions and market structure determine whether specification, evaluation, default setting, or scarce execution inputs generate rents and who captures them.

items.title: When Recognition Should Remain Silent
items.abstract: The Difference Between Being Remembered and Being Understood There is something profoundly human about the experience of being remembered. A familiar voice, a shared reference, or an acknowledgment of something that mattered in an earlier encounter can transform an otherwise ordinary exchange into one characterized by continuity. We recognize that our history has not disappeared simply because the previous conversation ended. In human relationships, this continuity can become a foundation for trust, familiarity, and the gradual development of shared understanding. Artificial intelligence is increasingly capable of participating in certain computational dimensions of this process. Persistent memory enables systems to retrieve earlier conversations, recognize recurring preferences, resume unfinished activities, and adapt their responses to the histories of individuals with whom they interact. As these capacities converge with multimodal perception and embodied robotics, artificial agents may also begin to initiate interactions based on what they believe they know about a person. Yet this development introduces a distinction that deserves greater attention: remembering someone accurately is not necessarily the same as understanding how to respond to them appropriately. Consider a companion robot that recognizes an individual returning home after a difficult day. Through previous encounters, the system may have learned that the person sometimes appreciates conversation or reassurance during stressful circumstances. Its memory could be accurate, its recognition successful, and its conversational response entirely consistent with earlier preferences. Nevertheless, initiating a supportive exchange may be precisely the wrong action if the person presently needs solitude, concentration, or the freedom to remain unobserved.

items.title: Where Polanyi Meets Galois: Tacit Knowing as an Algebro-Deterministic Operation, Toward Re-rooting AI-Generated Science
items.abstract: We argue that tacit knowing is better modelled as an operating regime of one memory substrate than as a kind of content. The substrate is VaCoAl, an algebro-deterministic XOR-and-shift hyperdimensional memory over GF(2), realized as CASRAM (commercial SRAM-CAM) and PyVaCoAl (DRAM-CAM).In VaCoAl/PyVaCoAl a directed acyclic graph (DAG) reads two ways. Repairing every collision (Rescue mode) makes the trace exactly auditable but ranks no path higher; tolerating collisions (Don't Care mode) yields a path-integrated confidence, CR$_2$, that silently favours direct routes. This audit-valuation complementarity is a formal counterpart of Polanyi's claim that tacit and explicit knowledge are not sharply divided. It separates contingent tacitness, which a new query brings out (AlphaGo's game tree), from regime-bound tacitness, statable only in a regime where it is gone (AlphaGo's hunches). (1) Polanyi's from-to structure reads as non-commutative binding, the Identikit as role-filler composition, recognition as majority-vote coincidence. (2) Explicating the valuation destroys it, as attending to his fingers can make Polanyi's pianist falter, yet a closed-form law states it. Polanyi, Nonaka, Tsoukas and Collins each capture part of this but narrowly; even Nonaka and von Krogh's continuum cannot tell contingent from regime-bound tacitness. (3) Collins's three tacit knowledges become strata, one outside the substrate. (4) Our mentor-student DAG is a tacit-transmission graph. (5) Terence Tao's remark that AI-solved problems spawn few follow-ups is diagnosed as rootless explicit knowledge: checkable results whose route no one can follow and that no one yet understands well enough to extend, teach or judge. To re-root them, LLMs generate, VaCoAl/PyVaCoAl keeps an auditable trace with its confidence, and people value, a role virtue epistemology shows cannot be offloaded. Testable predictions follow.
